soil-hist-059.title: Lunar regolith, the gunpowder-scented ground of the Moon
soil-hist-059.text: The Moon's finest dust reportedly tastes and smells of spent gunpowder. It belongs to the lunar regolith, the loose, unconsolidated material that covers the Moon's surface. Lunar soil usually means grains 1 cm across or less, and lunar dust the still finer fraction, under one millimeter. Earth's soils form through oxygen, water and life. The Moon's form by mechanical weathering instead, as impacts and charged particles from the Sun and interstellar space grind basaltic and anorthositic rock ever finer. By mass, half the soil is finer than 60–80 μm. Its density is about 1.5 g/cm³ and rises with depth. Seven elements make up 98–99% of it, led by oxygen at 41–45%. Its makeup follows the local bedrock, so it divides into highland and mare regolith. Plagioclase, olivine, pyroxenes and impact-melt glass dominate, with ice in permanently shaded craters. The fine grains are sharp, very sticky and electrically charged. Yet this hostile powder could become building material, such as {{ref:soil-hist-082}}, or a medium for growing plants.

soil-hist-067.title: Martian regolith, studied from afar under a rusty sky
soil-hist-067.text: No one has yet carried a scoop of Mars back to Earth. Everything known about its regolith, the fine blanket of loose, varied deposits covering the planet, comes from rovers and orbiters. Mars is covered with sand and dust and littered with rocks. Planet-wide storms lift fine dust that stays aloft and tints the sky reddish, the color of rusted iron minerals. Olivine, which weathers easily, is still present, so physical rather than chemical weathering seems to dominate now. Water and carbon dioxide ices are thought to lie frozen in the ground, and the Mars Odyssey orbiter measured water up to 5% by weight. In June 2008 the Phoenix lander found the soil basic, at pH 8.3, with nutrients such as magnesium, sodium, potassium and chloride. On October 17, 2012, Curiosity's first X-ray diffraction found feldspar, pyroxenes and olivine. The mix resembles the weathered basaltic soils of Hawaiian volcanoes. Researchers on Earth rely on stand-in materials such as Exolith Lab's MGS-1, and sample-return missions beginning with Mars 2020 should make them more accurate.

soil-hist-071.title: Fake moon soil, and the surprise it failed to predict
soil-hist-071.text: Before Apollo, crushed Earth rocks stood in for lunar soil. Some differed greatly from the real thing, and the Moon's pervasive sharp, fine dust came as a surprise. A lunar regolith simulant is an Earth material made to copy the Moon's regolith in its chemistry, mechanics, engineering behavior, minerals or particle sizes. Real samples are scarce, small and tainted by Earth's air, so researchers test digging and handling on simulants. Later simulants such as MLS-1 and JSC-1 came in highland and mare types., crushed and sieved from anorthosite or basalt to match Apollo and Luna samples. NASA and the Johnson Space Center developed JSC-1 in 1994 from a glass-rich basaltic ash. A version called JSC-1A, mixed into an alkaline solution, sets into a rock-like material as strong as conventional cements. The lunar scientist Larry Taylor criticized many simulants for poor quality control and money wasted on features with no documented purpose. Newer ones include Exolith Lab's LHS-1 and LMS-1, and LSS-ISAC1 from the Indian Space Research Organisation for its Chandrayaan program.

soil-hist-058.title: Astropedology, soil science for deep time and other worlds
soil-hist-058.text: Soil science has started looking up. Astropedology is the branch of pedology that studies very ancient paleosols, meteorites relevant to the origin of life, and soil systems on other planets. Its aim is to understand Earth's place in the universe. If soil is a planetary surface altered in place by biological, chemical or physical processes, a sharp question follows for Martian soils and old paleosols: were they alive? Work on other worlds has already changed the basics at home. Better understanding of soil formation elsewhere had an effect. In 2017 it helped lead the Soil Science Society of America to define soil as loose material altered at or near a planetary surface. The study of ancient soils underpins both this field, now reaching into exoplanet research, and the reconstruction of Earth's ancient ecosystems. Astropedology symposia are a new focus of soil science meetings.

soil-hist-079.title: Space weathering, the slow aging of airless worlds
soil-hist-079.text: With no air to shield them, the Moon, Mercury and the asteroids take the full force of space. Space weathering is the weathering of any object exposed to that harsh environment. Cosmic rays strike these airless bodies. The solar wind irradiates their surfaces, implants particles in them and sputters atoms away. Meteorites and micrometeorites bombard them. Much of what is known comes from lunar soils returned by Apollo. There, impacts and particles comminute, or crush, the soil, and also melt, sputter and vaporize it. Micrometeorite melt welds glass and mineral fragments into agglutinates, clumps that make up as much as 60 to 70% of mature lunar soils. Iron-bearing minerals such as olivine and pyroxene vaporize, then redeposit tiny blebs of metallic nanophase iron in agglutinates and in thin rims on grains. The effect shows from afar. As lunar soil matures it grows darker and redder, and its absorption bands grow shallower, so the bright rays of young craters fade with time. Reading remotely sensed data from planetary surfaces therefore requires understanding this process. On asteroids it works more slowly, yet grains that Hayabusa returned from Itokawa show definite alteration. Mercury should take a far harder beating. Impacts there are expected to make 13.5 times the melt and 19.5 times the vapor per unit area as on the Moon.

soil-hist-061.title: Moon dust, a hazard to machines and lungs
soil-hist-061.text: Apollo crews came in from moonwalks with coughs, throat irritation, watery eyes and blurred vision, though the symptoms cleared within 24 hours. Fine lunar dust is easily disturbed, and it can harm both equipment and crews. It darkens surfaces so they absorb more heat, abrades materials by friction, and degrades seals, lenses, solar panels, windows and wiring. In the lungs, reactive particles may cause respiratory disease, and long exposure possibly a disease similar to silicosis. A 2005 NASA study ranked dust the top challenge to study before a human Mars expedition, and its concerns apply equally to the Moon.

soil-hist-062.title: Bringing the Moon home, a few kilograms at a time
soil-hist-062.text: Apollo astronauts brought back some 360 kg of lunar rocks from six landing sites. Every returned sample carries a flaw. Earth's air and humidity contaminated the dust, which rusted and lost its chemical reactivity, so it no longer matches conditions on the Moon. After 1972 no new samples arrived until 16 December 2020. That day China's Chang'e 5 returned about 2 kg of lunar rock and soil, making China the third country to do so. In 2024 Chang'e 6 went further, returning samples from the far side of the Moon.

soil-hist-060.title: How the Moon makes soil without water or life
soil-hist-060.text: Lunar soil forms at a crawl. Crater production rates suggest it takes about 81 thousand years to overturn just the top 2 cm. This making and remaking is a case of {{ref:soil-hist-079}}. Each soil begins as a coarse, poorly sorted blanket of debris thrown out by impacts. Micrometeoroids then grind it finer, weld fragments into agglutinates with impact-melt glass, and add metallic iron, darkening it over time. Solar wind sputtering and cosmic ray spallation, which knocks fragments off atoms, keep altering the grains. Lava fire fountains also left glass beads, such as the orange soil Apollo 17 found at Shorty Crater and Apollo 15's green glass.

soil-hist-069.title: Perchlorates, the salts that make Martian soil toxic
soil-hist-069.text: The soil of Mars is laced with poison. In 2008 NASA's Phoenix lander first found perchlorates there, chlorine-bearing salts such as calcium perchlorate. Later landers and the Mars Odyssey orbiter showed they are spread across the planet. Levels of around 0.5% in the regolith are considered toxic to humans, and even trace amounts interfere with the thyroid. One source puts the level on Mars at 0.05% by weight. In a 2013 study, 0.5 g per liter of perchlorate cut leaf chlorophyll, root oxidizing power and plant size, and the salts built up in the leaves. The water hyacinth Eichhornia crassipes tolerated them and could help remove them. With no ozone layer, ultraviolet light reaches the ground and makes perchlorates more lethal to bacteria, while soil iron oxides and hydrogen peroxide add to their toxicity. Yet some bacteria adapt to perchlorate or even live off it. A NASA-funded project from 2022 is studying Dehalococcoides mccartyi to break the salts into chlorides and oxygen. Perchlorates may also make the organic molecules linked to life harder to detect.

soil-hist-083.title: Living off the land on the Moon and Mars
soil-hist-083.text: Future crews could lighten what they launch from Earth by living off the land. In situ resource utilization means collecting, processing and using materials found on the Moon, Mars or other bodies, in place of materials brought from home. It could supply life support, propellants, construction materials and energy. Anyone settling a planet or moon will need local building materials such as regolith. Water bound in regolith, ice or permafrost can be recovered by heating, though ice and permafrost may be harder than rock to mine. Heating lunar regolith above 900 °C in hydrogen gas pulls oxygen out of its iron oxide.

soil-hist-068.title: Is there soil on the Moon? It depends on the definition
soil-hist-068.text: Whether the Moon has soil depends on who is asked. Earth's usual definition includes organic content, which may not fit other worlds, and sources still disagree on what should replace it. Planetary scientists use a functional rule. Fragments of about 10 cm or more, larger than cobbles on the Wentworth scale, are rocks, and all other, typically loose material is soil. Planetary scientists also often adopt "medium for plant growth". A fuller definition calls soil any altered surface material that records its environmental history, with no life needed. Under Earth systems, many such soils would be Entisols in Soil Taxonomy or Regosols in the WRB, but applying those systems to such different settings is debatable. An alternative would put all non-Earth soils in a new group, tentatively called Astrosols.

soil-hist-070.title: Martian dust, lifted again and again
soil-hist-070.text: On Mars, dust that settles rarely stays put. Martian dust is the finest fraction of the regolith, under 30 micrometers across, and much of it rides in the atmosphere as particles about 3 μm across. On Earth, soil moisture and oceans gather settled dust into larger particles. Neither works on Mars, so deposited dust is free to rise again. Dust from the 2001 global storms stayed aloft only 0.6 years, against about two years for Mount Pinatubo's. Plagioclase feldspar and zeolite dominate it, which suggests it is ground mechanically from basaltic rock with little chemical alteration. One study found that it reacts with water to form highly reactive molecules, like those that cause lung disease in quartz miners.

soil-hist-082.title: Lunarcrete, concrete made from the Moon itself
soil-hist-082.text: Lunarcrete is a proposed concrete-like material made from lunar regolith to cut the cost of construction there. Like concrete it would use aggregate, water and cement, with regolith as the aggregate and cement from calcium-rich lunar rock. In 1986 Lin and colleagues made lunarcrete from 40 g of Apollo 16 regolith, and it withstood 75 MPa of compression. A waterless version binds regolith simulant with sulfur. A mix of 65% JSC-1 simulant and 35% sulfur averaged 33.8 MPa. A stranger recipe, AstroCrete, proposed for the Moon or Mars, binds regolith with human serum albumin, a protein from blood.

soil-hist-081.title: Making Mars soil on Earth
soil-hist-081.text: The first stand-in for Mars soil came from Hawaii. JSC Mars-1, made at NASA's Johnson Space Center in 1998, was palagonitic tephra: volcanic ash altered at low temperature. A Martian regolith simulant mimics the chemistry and mechanics of Martian regolith for research and prototype testing. Mojave Mars Simulant, from 2007, was crushed basalt with minimal weathering, so unlike the clay-like JSC Mars-1 it did not attract water. From 2018, MGS-1 became the first mineralogically accurate simulant, a mix of pure minerals matched to the Rocknest soil analyzed by Curiosity in Gale crater. No simulant includes the perchlorates Phoenix found in 2008, though users can add the salts. Their fine particles and crystalline silica pose some health risk.

soil-hist-080.title: Impact gardening, how meteorites till the Moon
soil-hist-080.text: The Moon's soil is tilled, but by meteorites rather than plows. Airless moons and similar bodies have almost no erosion, so impact debris builds up at the surface as a rough soil, the regolith. Later impacts, especially by micrometeorites, stir and mix it. This is impact gardening, called lunar gardening on the Moon. The top centimeter of the Moon was long thought to overturn every 10 million years. A 2016 LRO study of impact ejecta put it closer to 80,000 years.

soil-hist-065.title: Archean paleosols and early Earth's hints of soil life
soil-hist-065.text: Soils formed 3.42 to 3.46 billion years ago may carry faint signs of life. Archean paleosols are soils preserved from early Earth's Archean eon, and they give circumstantial evidence of life in soils at that time. Profiles from the Pilbara region of northwestern Australia show distinct depletion of phosphorus. Sulfates may hold another clue. Sulfur bacteria commonly oxidize sulfur to sulfates such as gypsum and barite, minerals of today's acid sulfate soils. Their work is a possible reason for sulfate build-up in Archean paleosols.

soil-hist-064.title: Can a garden grow in moon dust?
soil-hist-064.text: Lunar and Martian soils appear to hold every essential plant mineral in sufficient amounts, with one possible exception. Reactive nitrogen may be short, since Mars Pathfinder could not detect it. Nitrogen-fixing species could make up the shortfall, but fixation needs nitrogen from the air, absent on the Moon and only a trace on Mars. In a large controlled experiment, plants germinated and grew for 50 days on Mars and Moon soil simulants without added nutrients., doing much better on the Mars simulant. Plants struggle in real lunar soil, so long missions may need imported Earth soil, chemically treated regolith or plants bred for it.

soil-hist-063.title: Ancient soils on Mars, and the open question of life
soil-hist-063.text: In Gale Crater, the Curiosity rover found features much like Earth's soil horizons and structures. They included blocky angular peds, sand wedges, a shallow gypsic horizon and vesicular structure. These are Martian paleosols, ancient soils recognized by rovers and orbiters. The Yellowknife Bay paleosols, about 3.7 billion years old, show olivine weathering to smectite. They record a shift from possibly warm and wet to extremely cold and arid. Orbiters have detected phyllosilicate clays at thousands of sites dated to 4.0–3.7 billion years ago. Either hydrothermal activity or surface weathering and soil formation could explain them. Vesicular structures like those made by microbial gas in Earth's desert soils occur on Mars, but definitive evidence of life there is still lacking.

soil-hist-066.title: Was life born in the soil?
soil-hist-066.text: Life may have begun in the ground. On this idea, water held between clay grains forms countless microscopic reaction chambers where life evolved. These chambers may also promote the making of organic compounds by mechanisms shown in the Miller–Urey experiment. Soil would have kept the process going. Clayey and organic soils resist erosion, so they keep producing clay and organic matter, and early single-celled life would also have bound the soil. The idea extends {{ref:soil-chem-083}}. And the weathering cycle still supplies the ingredients that life requires.

openers.soils-beyond-earth: The Moon and Mars have ground underfoot too, and this last chapter asks what it is. The Moon wears a blanket of loose material, made and constantly altered by impacts and space radiation. Mars has a fine layer of loose, varied deposits, laced with chlorine-bearing salts toxic enough to matter. Space missions, beginning with Apollo, have carried lunar rock and regolith back to Earth, and Earth materials are made to stand in for the rest. Beneath it all runs an unsettled question: whether Earth's definition of soil, with its organic content, fits other worlds at all.

reviews.soils-beyond-earth: The Moon and Mars both wear regolith, but neither made it the way Earth makes soil. On the Moon, impacts and charged particles grind rock finer and weld it into agglutinates, while impact gardening stirs the result over tens of thousands of years. Mars adds wind-lifted dust and perchlorates, and rovers, simulants and returned lunar samples show what settlers would face, from dust in the lungs to lunarcrete and gardens grown in simulant. Paleosols on Mars and in Earth's Archean rocks raise astropedology's central question: were these soils ever alive? That work has fed back home, helping redefine soil in 2017 as loose material altered at or near a planetary surface, though sources still disagree on what soil means off Earth.
